name: Question 20
problem:
$$
{y}^{‴}-2{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-8y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\,{{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}
$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{u}_{1}(x){e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{3}(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

What is the function ${u}_{2}(x)?$
worked_solution:
According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}+{u}_{3}{y}_{3},\,{u}_{i}=(-1)^{3-i}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,\,i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{2}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{3}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 2{e}^{2x} & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ 4{e}^{2x} & -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{2x}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 2 & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ 4 & -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{2x}[(8{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+8{cos}^{2}⁡(2x))-2(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))+4(2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x))] \\  & ={e}^{2x}[8-2(0)+4(2)] \\  & =16{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find ${u}_{2},$ we compute the determinant ${W}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{2}(x) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x} & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 2{e}^{2x} & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\  & =2{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =(-1)^{3-2}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{2}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\cdot 2{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}{16{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\int [{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)]\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{32}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form y(x)=Ae2x+Bcos⁡(2x)+Csin⁡(2x)+u1(x)e2x+u2(x)cos⁡(2x)+u3(x)sin⁡(2x). What is the function u2(x)?

EXPLANATION

According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

yp=u1y1+u2y2+u3y3,ui=(−1)3−i∫g(x)Wi(x)W(x)dx,i=1,2,3,

where g(x) is the forcing term, W(x) is the Wronskian of y1,y2,y3, and

W1(x)=|y2y3y2′y3′|,W2(x)=|y1y3y1′y3′|,W3(x)=|y1y2y1′y2′|.

In our case, the forcing term is g(x)=cos⁡(2x)+sin⁡(2x). Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions y1=e2x,y2=cos⁡(2x),y3=sin⁡(2x).

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions y1, y2, and y3 are independent by computing the Wronskian:

W(x)=W(y1,y2,y3)=|e2xcos⁡(2x)sin⁡(2x)2e2x−2sin⁡(2x)2cos⁡(2x)4e2x−4cos⁡(2x)−4sin⁡(2x)|=e2x⋅|1cos⁡(2x)sin⁡(2x)2−2sin⁡(2x)2cos⁡(2x)4−4cos⁡(2x)−4sin⁡(2x)|=e2x[(8sin2⁡(2x)+8cos2⁡(2x))−2(−4sin⁡(2x)cos⁡(2x)+4sin⁡(2x)cos⁡(2x))+4(2sin2⁡(2x)+2cos2⁡(2x))]=e2x[8−2(0)+4(2)]=16e2x

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions y1, y2, and y3 are linearly independent.

Now, to find u2, we compute the determinant W2(x):

W2(x)=|y1y3y1′y3′|=|e2xsin⁡(2x)2e2x2cos⁡(2x)|=2e2xcos⁡(2x)−2e2xsin⁡(2x)=2e2x(cos⁡(2x)−sin⁡(2x))

Therefore, we have

u2(x)=(−1)3−2∫g(x)W2(x)W(x)dx=−∫(cos⁡(2x)+sin⁡(2x))⋅2e2x(cos⁡(2x)−sin⁡(2x))16e2xdx=−18∫[cos2⁡(2x)−sin2⁡(2x)]dx=−18∫cos⁡(4x)dx=−18⋅14sin⁡(4x)=−132sin⁡(4x).
